newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India sulks as it remembers Gandhi values.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India sulks as it remembers Gandhi values.

text.p: When a thin, bespectacled man dressed in a loincloth spoke persuasively of truth, morality and non-violence half a century ago, the whole of India listened.
But 50 years after Mahatma Gandhi roused the nation's conscience, Indians are staring in disbelief at the moral decay that is eating away at its social fabric.

As the country prepares to celebrate its 50th anniversary of freedom from British colonial rule, Indians fondly remember the spiritual father of independent India and recoil in horror at political and bureaucratic corruption surrounding them.

"It is the people of the country who have lost their moral integrity and they have not protected against this kind of moral laxity and that is today's difficulty," says Sumitra Gandhi Kulkarni, one of Gandhi's granddaughters.
INDIA PLAGUED BY POLITICAL CORRUPTION
The party that Gandhi once belonged to, Congress, was battered in India's last general elections after many of its leaders were named in a series of corruption cases.
More than half a dozen ministers of the 112-year-old Congress, once synonymous with the freedom movement, resigned last year after being named in a money-laundering scandal.

In stark contrast to modern politicians, Gandhi often chose to live in slums among sweepers who belonged at the bottom of Hinduism's caste ladder. Society referred to them as untouchables -- Gandhi, who said untouchability was a crime against god and mankind, called them "Harijans," or children of god.

He often slept on the floor and cleaned his own latrine -- unusual for a London-educated barrister who rubbed shoulders with heads of governments and millionaires, often winning their political and financial support for India's freedom movement.

India's independence on August 15, 1947, followed decades of struggle against colonial rule. Five-and-a-half months later, Gandhi was assassinated at a prayer meeting by a man who bent down to touch his feet, as if to seek Gandhi's blessings, before shooting him dead.
POLITICAL CORRUPTION A REFLECTION OF SOCIETY
Kulkarni said pre-independence India was a country with tremendous poverty but brimming with enthusiasm and dedication.
"Over the years, I find a serious erosion in these basic qualities of our countrymen," she said.

"(For) all these crises, all these scams and scandals I do not hold the government responsible," Kulkarni told Reuters, referring to the spate of political corruption scandals. "(But) politicians are a part of society and the society condoned it. It was not vigilant enough of its freedom and dignity."

Clad in a white sari made of handspun cotton, popularised by Gandhi as a symbol of self-reliance and widely worn by Indian politicians who proudly claim to have inherited his mantle, Kulkarni said Indians' attitudes would change once they realised where they were heading.
MORAL DEGENERATION INEVITABLE, SAY HISTORIANS
Historians say the degeneration of moral values is an inevitable consequence of victory in an ideological struggle.
"Once the struggle is over, its benefits have to be reaped," said S.D. Muni, professor in the department of South Asian Studies at the Jawaharlal Nehru University.
He said that after any prolonged struggle, the focus always shifts to individual well-being, as it had in India and several other countries.
Muni said it would be unfair to seek a comparison with standards set during the freedom movement and present-day values.
Gandhi as a "real man" saw this degeneration happening during his life time, he added.
To Gandhi, the blood-stained partition of British India into India and Pakistan was a real shock. This, in Gandhi's mind was a degeneration, Muni said.
"Today, we see it in full bloom corrupting politics," Muni added.
But he said such degeneration had set in in countries around the world, such as China and the former Soviet Union. "Mao never dreamt of it (degeneration), Lenin never dreamt of it," he added.
But Muni said he was an optimist who expected the birth of an antithesis to moral degeneration. "History creates new values. Perhaps we will have new values," he added.
